terms.HTTP: HTTP semantics (RFC 9110) are shared by every version: methods with defined safety and idempotency, status code classes, header fields, content negotiation and conditional requests via ETag and If-None-Match. The wire format differs: HTTP/1.1 is text over TCP, HTTP/2 multiplexes binary frames over one TCP connection with HPACK header compression, and HTTP/3 runs over QUIC on UDP, removing TCP head-of-line blocking. Statelessness enables horizontal scaling, with state moved into cookies, tokens or shared stores. Caching (RFC 9111) via Cache-Control, Vary and validators is a large part of web performance. Common bugs include GET with side effects, 200 responses for errors, and request smuggling from inconsistent Content-Length handling between proxies.
terms.TLS handshake: In TLS 1.3 the client sends supported cipher suites and a key share (commonly X25519, increasingly hybrid post-quantum X25519MLKEM768) in ClientHello. The server replies with its share, and everything after ServerHello is encrypted, including the certificate and CertificateVerify signature. Ephemeral Diffie-Hellman provides forward secrecy. The client validates the chain to a trusted root, the hostname against the Subject Alternative Name, and validity dates. Resumption with pre-shared keys enables 0-RTT data, which is replayable and should carry only idempotent requests. SNI leaks the hostname unless Encrypted Client Hello is used. TLS 1.0/1.1 are deprecated; mutual TLS adds client certificates for service-to-service authentication.
terms.TCP: TCP provides a reliable, ordered byte stream with no message boundaries, so applications must frame messages. Random initial sequence numbers are exchanged in the SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK handshake; ACKs are cumulative, and loss triggers retransmission after a timeout or three duplicate ACKs. Flow control uses the receiver window; congestion control (CUBIC, BBR) adapts the sending rate. A connection is identified by the 5-tuple of protocol, source and destination IPs and ports. Closing leaves the active closer in TIME_WAIT. Costs are a round trip before data and head-of-line blocking, which is why QUIC reimplements reliability per stream over UDP. SYN cookies defend against SYN floods.
terms.DNS: Resolution goes stub resolver -> recursive resolver -> root -> TLD -> authoritative server, with every answer, including negative NXDOMAIN answers, cached for its TTL. Queries use UDP port 53, falling back to TCP for large responses. A CNAME cannot coexist with other records at the zone apex, hence provider ALIAS records. HTTPS/SVCB records can advertise HTTP/3 and ECH keys. DNSSEC authenticates answers with signatures; DoH and DoT encrypt queries. Operational lessons: lower TTLs before migrations, remember that clients and runtimes may cache beyond TTL, and treat DNS as a frequent root cause of outages. DNS rebinding attacks abuse short TTLs to bypass same-origin and SSRF filters.
terms.CIDR notation: CIDR replaced classful A/B/C networks in 1993 to slow IPv4 exhaustion and shrink routing tables through aggregation. A /n prefix leaves 2^(32-n) addresses; membership is tested by ANDing the address with the mask, and routers forward by longest prefix match, so a /24 route overrides a covering /16. Traditionally a subnet's first and last addresses are reserved (network and broadcast); clouds reserve more, AWS five per subnet. RFC 1918 private ranges are 10/8, 172.16/12 and 192.168/16, and 100.64/10 is carrier-grade NAT space. IPv6 uses the same notation, with /64 the standard subnet size. Overlapping VPC ranges block later peering, so plan address space early.
terms.Unix pipe: A pipe is a kernel buffer (64 KB by default on Linux) with a write end and a read end; the shell forks each stage and wires stdout of one to stdin of the next with dup2. Stages run concurrently, and a full buffer blocks the writer, giving natural backpressure; when the reader exits, the writer gets SIGPIPE. The pipeline's exit status is the last stage's unless set -o pipefail is on. stderr is not piped by default; 2>&1 or |& merges it. Named pipes (mkfifo) give pipes a filesystem path. Process substitution <(cmd) exposes a pipe as a file path, enabling commands like diff <(sort a) <(sort b).
terms.SQL injection: Injection occurs whenever untrusted input reaches an interpreter as code. Variants include classic in-band (UNION-based), error-based, blind boolean or time-based extraction, and second-order injection where stored data is later concatenated unsafely. Prepared statements parse the query before binding values, making structure immune to input; they cannot parameterize identifiers, so table names, columns and sort directions need allowlists. ORMs are safe until raw-SQL escape hatches are used. Defense in depth adds least-privilege database accounts, no stack traces in responses, and WAF rules as a backstop, not a fix. The same pattern applies to shell, LDAP, NoSQL operators and template injection.
terms.Cross-site scripting: XSS has stored, reflected and DOM-based forms; all run attacker JavaScript in the victim's origin, defeating the same-origin policy. Defenses are context-aware encoding (HTML body, attribute, URL and JavaScript contexts differ), safe framework defaults, sanitizing user-supplied HTML with a vetted library like DOMPurify, and a strict Content-Security-Policy using nonces or hashes with no unsafe-inline. Trusted Types can lock down DOM sinks like innerHTML. HttpOnly cookies limit session theft, but XSS can still act as the user within the page. Dangerous sinks include innerHTML, document.write, eval, javascript: URLs and React's dangerouslySetInnerHTML.
terms.JSON Web Token: A JWT (RFC 7519) is usually a JWS: base64url header and payload signed with HMAC (HS256) or asymmetric keys (RS256, ES256, EdDSA). JWE adds encryption but is rarer. Known pitfalls: accepting alg none, algorithm confusion where an RS256 public key is used as an HS256 secret, trusting kid or jku headers to fetch attacker keys, and skipping exp, nbf, iss or aud checks. Revocation requires short lifetimes, rotating refresh tokens with reuse detection, or a denylist that reintroduces state. Storage is a trade-off: localStorage is exposed to XSS, cookies to CSRF. For first-party web sessions, opaque server-side session IDs are often simpler and safer.
terms.Race condition: A data race is unsynchronized concurrent access with at least one write; a race condition is any timing-dependent correctness bug, including check-then-act sequences built from individually atomic steps. Races arise across threads, processes, async tasks and distributed services, for example two servers both selling the last item. Compilers and CPUs reorder memory operations, so without synchronization visibility is not guaranteed; language memory models define happens-before rules. Races are nondeterministic and often hidden by testing, so use ThreadSanitizer or go test -race, stress tests, and designs that avoid shared mutable state. In databases, use transactions, SELECT ... FOR UPDATE, or optimistic version checks.
terms.Mutex: A mutex provides mutual exclusion plus memory visibility: writes before unlock are visible after the next lock. Implementations spin briefly then sleep in the kernel (futexes on Linux), so uncontended locking costs tens of nanoseconds while contention costs context switches. Variants include reentrant locks, read-write locks, semaphores and fair locks that prevent starvation. Always release in finally or with RAII or a context manager. Keep critical sections short and never hold a lock across I/O or callbacks into unknown code. Alternatives are atomics and compare-and-swap, single-owner designs with queues, and immutable data. Lock ordering discipline prevents deadlock when several locks are needed.
terms.Deadlock: Coffman et al. (1971) showed deadlock requires mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption and circular wait simultaneously. Prevention removes one: global lock ordering kills circular wait, acquiring all locks atomically kills hold and wait, and try-lock with timeout and back-off approximates preemption at the risk of livelock. Avoidance algorithms like the Banker's algorithm need advance knowledge of resource needs and are rare in practice. Detection builds a wait-for graph and breaks cycles, which is what databases do by aborting a victim transaction, so applications must retry. Diagnose hangs with thread dumps showing held and awaited locks. Distributed deadlocks across services usually surface as timeouts.
